references.text: John's testimony is introduced earlier in the prologue: he came to testify about the light. Here in verse 19, the actual content of this testimony begins to unfold ([ref:Joh 1:6-8|John 1:6-8]).
Jesus himself refers back to John's testimony and confirms that the Jews sent messengers to him, and that he testified to the truth ([ref:Joh 5:33-35|John 5:33-35]).
The immediate continuation of John's testimony, where he confesses that he is not the Messiah, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet, but a voice crying out in the wilderness ([ref:Joh 1:20-27|John 1:20-27]).
Malachi prophesies about a messenger who will be sent to prepare the way – background for why the Jews sent priests and Levites to ask John about his identity ([ref:Mal 3:1|Malachi 3:1]).

The promise of a prophet like Moses whom the Lord will raise up – this was one of the messianic expectations behind the question "Who are you?" that was asked of John ([ref:5 Mos 18:15-18|Deuteronomy 18:15-18]).
The prophecy about "a voice crying out in the wilderness", which John the Baptist identifies with when he answers the question about who he is ([ref:Jes 40:3|Isaiah 40:3]).
Also in Luke, the people's expectation that John might be the Messiah is described, explaining why the authorities sent a delegation to investigate his identity ([ref:Luk 3:15-16|Luke 3:15-16]).
John the Baptist later reminds his own disciples that he had said he was not the Christ, but was sent ahead of him – a reference back to this testimony ([ref:Joh 3:28|John 3:28]).
